title: A Difficult Conversation
focus: 区分意图与影响，协商工作边界
story:
At ten twenty-eight, I stand outside the small meeting room with a notebook that contains three opening sentences. All three sound reasonable on paper. None sounds like something I can say without reading.

Daniel arrives carrying coffee and a charging cable. “I've got half an hour,” he says.

“That should be enough.”

I sit where I can see the door, then wonder why that matters. He plugs in his laptop but leaves it closed.

“I want to explain what happened for me yesterday,” I begin. “When you said you needed more than reasons the pilot might go wrong, I felt that the choices I'd prepared weren't being considered.”

He looks down at his cup. “I was frustrated.”

“I could tell. I also became less willing to explain the remaining risks. That concerns me, because explaining them is part of my job.”

The room becomes very quiet. In the corridor, a trolley wheel makes a repeated squeak. I resist the urge to soften everything I have said with a quick apology.

Daniel takes the lid off his coffee. “I didn't mean that you should hide risks.”

“I don't think you did. I'm describing the effect, not guessing your intention.”

He nods once. “Fair.”

I had imagined a longer disagreement. The small agreement leaves me briefly without a next sentence.

“What I need,” he continues, “is a recommendation that I can take to the client and defend. The budget is limited. The centre has made arrangements. If all I say is that engineering isn't comfortable, I haven't given anyone a decision they can act on.”

“I agree. I recommend the smaller supervised pilot, provided we meet the essential checks. If we don't, I recommend a delay.”

“That still sounds conditional.”

“It is conditional. I can't honestly remove the conditions before we've checked them.”

He leans back. I can see the beginning of an answer, and then a decision to wait.

I explain the checks one by one: staff access, correct handling of a class-time change, the notification tests, a practised fallback, and a named person who can stop the pilot. We do not need every report or every improvement. We do need the people at the desk to know what happens when a step fails.

Daniel asks which checks are complete and which are not. This question is easier. I show him the evidence and the remaining owners. He points out that one owner has not agreed to the deadline. He is right. I circle the name instead of defending the document.

Then he asks, “Has the internal test problem made you too cautious?”

My first reaction is to deny it. I can still see the repeated emails in the test inbox. I remember explaining that I had assumed a new saved change should also send notices for earlier changes again. Nobody had asked me to make that assumption.

“It has made me more cautious,” I say. “I'm not sure every part of that caution is useful. But the duplicate-message checks are based on a specific failure. The staff-access concern comes from Priya. They aren't all the same kind of worry.”

“That's helpful.” He turns the notebook towards himself. “We should separate evidence from anxiety. Including mine.”

I look up.

“I worry that another delay will damage the client's trust,” he says. “I also worry about using the whole budget before we learn anything. Sometimes I push for a date because a date makes everyone organise the work.”

“And sometimes I stay quiet because I think you'll decide I'm difficult.”

“Then I assume you've agreed.”

We both stop. It is an ordinary exchange, with no dramatic revelation, but it describes months of small misunderstandings better than either of our documents.

We agree on a practical change. When a decision affects my work, I will state agreement, disagreement, or what I still need to check. Daniel will ask for that response rather than treating the absence of an objection as approval. Neither of us promises to do it perfectly.

He asks for the revised recommendation by mid-afternoon. I say I can complete it if the reporting task moves to tomorrow. He checks the schedule and accepts the trade-off.

As I gather my notebook, he says, “You were right to ask for this meeting.”

“Next time I'd prefer to ask before I'm upset.”

“That would probably help both of us.”

Back at my desk I ring the colleague whose work I offered to fit into the morning. She lets me finish. “Have you already told Daniel I can do that?”

I've spent half an hour asking him to stop taking my silence for agreement. She wasn't even in the room.

“I gave him a time. I should have rung you first.”

She can prepare an example before lunch. Checking it will take another pair of eyes after lunch. She sounds cheerful until I suggest the two things could share a line on the schedule.

“Two lines, please. Last time I gave somebody half a job they thanked me and showed the half to the client.”

When Daniel gets the new times he comes over in person. People nearby stop typing. I think he is going to ask me to find another way.

“Does she know about these times?”

“She gave them to me.”

He reads them again. “Right. I'll change what I told Elena.”

The typing starts up. I hadn't realised he had already spoken to Elena, or that he would have to make a second call because I had wanted to sound certain in the first. For a while he stays at his desk with his jacket on, waiting for London to pick up.

phrases.en: I’m describing the effect, not guessing your intention.
phrases.zh: 区分实际影响与动机推测

phrases.en: What I need is a recommendation.
phrases.zh: 明确自己真正需要的产出

phrases.en: I can’t honestly remove the conditions.
phrases.zh: 守住依据事实表达的边界

phrases.en: We should separate evidence from anxiety.
I can do that if the other task moves.
phrases.zh: 说明承诺所依赖的取舍

practice.grammar: 练习强调句 What I need is...，用于把抱怨转成需求。例：What I need is a clear decision. 分别用时间、信息、反馈作为内容造句并说出来。
practice.pronunciation: 读 I felt / that the choices I’d prepared / weren’t being considered. 在 felt 后稍停，重读 choices 和 considered；保持音量稳定，练习表达不满而不抢话。

questions.a: Daniel’s comment made him less willing to explain the remaining risks.

questions.q: Why does a colleague ask for two lines on the schedule?
questions.a: Preparing an example and checking it finish at different times, and an unfinished example has reached a client before.

questions.q: What communication change do they agree to try?
questions.a: Andy will state his position explicitly, and Daniel will ask rather than assume silence means agreement.

roleplay.context: 你扮演 Andy，私下与 Daniel 讨论一次令人不舒服的交流。先描述事实，再说明影响与需求。

turns.line: I never asked you to hide risks.
turns.cue: 承认他的意图说明，并解释那句话对你的实际影响

turns.line: I still need a recommendation I can defend.
turns.cue: 给出明确但有条件的建议

turns.line: Can you finish this and the reporting task today?
turns.cue: 说明工作取舍，协商一个真实可交付的安排

practice.transfer: 准备一次与合租室友讨论噪声的英语对话。使用具体事件、实际影响、可执行请求三个部分，不推测对方性格或动机；开口演练两种可能回应。
practice.retell: 用两到三分钟复述双方各自压力、Andy 承认的担忧，以及最后的具体约定。加入一个你认为对话可能恶化、但实际没有恶化的节点。

translations.22-1: 十点二十八分，我站在小会议室外，笔记本里写着三句开场白。
translations.22-2: 三句写在纸上都挺像样。
translations.22-3: 但没有一句像是我能不看本子就自然说出口的。
translations.22-4: Daniel拿着咖啡和一根充电线走来。
translations.22-7: 我坐在能看见门的位置，然后又想，这有什么要紧的？
translations.22-8: 他给电脑插上电，却没有打开。
translations.22-9: “我想说说昨天那件事对我的影响。”我开口道。
translations.22-10: “你说，你需要的不只是试点可能出问题的理由，那时我觉得，自己准备的几个选择并没有被认真考虑。”
translations.22-14: 那也让我不太愿意继续解释剩下的风险。
translations.22-15: 这让我担心，因为讲清这些风险本来就是我的职责。”
translations.22-17: 走廊上，一辆推车的轮子反复发出吱呀声。
translations.22-18: 我忍住了马上道歉、把刚才那些话都说软一些的冲动。
translations.22-22: 我是在说它造成的影响，不是在猜你的动机。”
translations.22-26: 这小小的认同，反倒让我一时不知道下一句该说什么。
translations.22-27: “我需要的，”他继续说，“是一个能拿给客户、也能说明理由的建议。
translations.22-30: 如果我只说工程团队不放心，那就没有给任何人一个可以据此行动的决定。”
translations.22-32: 我的建议是，在通过必要检查的前提下，开展规模较小、有人监督的试点。
translations.22-36: 检查还没做完，我没法诚实地把这些条件删掉。”
translations.22-38: 我看得出他正要回答，随后又决定先等一等。
translations.22-39: 我逐项解释检查内容：工作人员的登录权限、课程时间修改是否处理正确、通知测试、演练过的备用流程，以及明确指定一位有权叫停试点的人。
translations.22-40: 我们不需要每一份报表、每一项改进都完成。
translations.22-41: 但我们确实需要前台人员知道，某一步失败时该怎么办。
translations.22-42: Daniel问哪些检查已经完成，哪些还没完成。
translations.22-44: 我给他看了证据和剩余事项的负责人。
translations.22-45: 他指出，有一位负责人还没有同意截止时间。
translations.22-47: 我把名字圈了起来，没有急着为文档辩护。
translations.22-48: 然后他问：“内部测试出的那个问题，是不是让你太谨慎了？”
translations.22-50: 那些重复的邮件，仿佛还在测试收件箱里。
translations.22-51: 我记得自己当时解释说，我以为每次保存新修改，也应该再发一遍之前修改的通知。
translations.22-52: 没有人要求我作出这个假设。
translations.22-54: “我也不确定这些谨慎是不是全都有用。
translations.22-55: 但重复消息的检查，是基于一次具体的故障。
translations.22-56: 工作人员账号的问题，是Priya提出来的。
translations.22-57: 这些担心并不全是一回事。”
translations.22-60: “我们应该把证据和焦虑分开。
translations.22-63: “我担心再推迟一次，会损害客户的信任。”他说。
translations.22-64: “也担心我们还没获得什么经验，预算就已经用完了。
translations.22-65: 有时候我催着定日期，是因为日期能促使大家把工作组织起来。”
translations.22-66: “而有时候我不说话，是因为担心你会觉得我难合作。”
translations.22-69: 这是一段普通的对话，没有什么惊人的领悟，却比我们任何一份文档都更准确地描述了几个月来的种种小误会。
translations.22-70: 我们约定了一项实际的改变。
translations.22-71: 以后，当决定影响到我的工作时，我会明确说出同意、不同意，或还有什么需要检查。
translations.22-72: Daniel会主动询问我的回应，而不是把没有反对当成批准。
translations.22-73: 我们都没有保证自己能做得完美。
translations.22-74: 他希望我在下午中段之前交给他修改后的建议。
translations.22-75: 我说，如果把报表任务挪到明天，我就能完成。
translations.22-76: 他看了看安排，接受了这个取舍。
translations.22-77: 我收拾笔记本时，他说：“你提出开这个会，是对的。”
translations.22-78: “下次我希望能在自己难受之前就提出来。”
translations.22-80: 回到工位，我打给那位同事。之前是我提议把她的工作塞进上午的。
translations.22-83: 我刚刚花了半小时，请他别再把我的沉默当成同意。
translations.22-84: 可她当时甚至都不在会议室里。
translations.22-87: 她能在午饭前准备好一个示例。
translations.22-88: 至于检查，要等午饭后再找个人过目。
translations.22-89: 她本来说得挺轻快，直到我提议在进度表上把两件事并成一行。
translations.22-91: 上次我把做了一半的东西交出去，人家道了谢，转头就拿那一半给客户看了。”
translations.22-92: Daniel收到新时间，亲自走了过来。
translations.22-93: 附近的人都停下了打字的手。
translations.22-94: 我以为他要叫我另想办法。
translations.22-97: 他把那几个时间又读了一遍。
translations.22-101: 我这才知道他已经跟Elena说过了，就因为我头一回想把话说得有把握，他现在还得再打一次电话。
translations.22-102: 他穿着外套在工位上坐了一阵，等伦敦那头接电话。
